clinical_safety.purpose: Clinical decision support and retrieval reference; not a substitute for a clinician, local protocols, or emergency services.
clinical_safety.audience_note: Separate lay first aid from clinician-only interventions. Medication lists are not patient-specific prescriptions.
medication_guardrails: Confirm patient identity, age, weight when relevant, allergies, pregnancy status, renal/hepatic function, current medicines, contraindications, and local formulary.
Use current institutional protocols and product labels for exact dosing, preparation, route, monitoring, and contraindications.
Do not delay emergency transport, imaging, reperfusion, CPR, or specialist review to search this knowledge base.
Do not give oral food, drink, or medicines to a person with possible stroke until swallowing safety is assessed.
Medication use in children, pregnancy, older adults, renal impairment, and critical illness requires extra caution and clinician oversight.
clinical_safety.review_status: Draft reference compiled from the sources listed in each file. Must be reviewed and signed off by the institution's clinical lead before clinical deployment.
clinical_safety.jurisdiction_note: Designed as a general reference with India-relevant emergency number context; confirm local emergency numbers, referral pathways, drug availability, and national guidelines.

scope: Child choking age 1 year and older

emergency_triggers: Cannot breathe, speak, cry, or cough effectively
Silent or weak cough, blue/grey lips or skin, collapse or reduced consciousness
Suspected button battery or multiple magnet ingestion
Persistent cough, wheeze, drooling, swallowing difficulty, or chest/abdominal pain after an event
immediate_action: Call the local emergency number; in India, 112 is the national emergency number (108 ambulance availability may vary by state).
If effective coughing or crying continues, encourage coughing and observe closely.
For severe obstruction, follow age-specific first-aid steps below and follow dispatcher instructions.
do_not: Never perform a blind finger sweep.
Do not give food or drink to dislodge an object.
Do not use abdominal thrusts on an infant under 1 year.
Do not delay emergency assessment for button batteries or multiple magnets.

recognition: Unable to cry, breathe or cough effectively
steps: Call for help and activate emergency response.
Give up to 5 back blows with the infant supported face-down, head lower than chest, supporting the head and jaw.
If obstruction persists, turn face-up and give up to 5 chest thrusts using two fingers on the lower half of the breastbone; avoid the tip of the breastbone.
Repeat cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts.
Remove an object only if clearly visible.
If unresponsive and not breathing normally, place on a firm surface, activate emergency response, and begin infant CPR; look for a visible object when opening the airway.
pathways.aftercare: Urgent medical assessment is recommended after a significant choking episode, especially if thrusts were needed or symptoms persist.

recognition: Unable to speak, cough or breathe effectively
steps: Call for help and activate emergency response.
Lean the child forward and give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades.
If obstruction persists, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts, above the navel and below the breastbone; adapt technique to the child's size.
Repeat 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the obstruction clears or the child becomes unresponsive.
If unresponsive, lower to a firm surface, call emergency services, and begin CPR; remove only visible objects.
pathways.aftercare: Medical review after abdominal thrusts is important because internal injury can occur.

steps: Seat children upright during meals and supervise eating.
Avoid age-inappropriate choking hazards; cut round foods such as grapes and sausages lengthwise into small pieces and modify hard foods to safe textures.
Keep coins, button batteries, magnets, balloons and small objects out of reach.
Suspected button battery or multiple magnet ingestion is an emergency even if the child appears well. Do not induce vomiting. Follow poison-control/emergency instructions.

diagnosis_and_assessment.lay_assessment: Assess ability to cough, speak, cry and breathe; do not delay action to perform a detailed examination.
clinical_assessment: Airway, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation and consciousness
History of object/food, timing, witnessed aspiration and interventions
Examination for stridor, wheeze, unilateral reduced air entry, drooling or trauma
Imaging or bronchoscopy only as directed by the treating clinician; normal initial imaging does not always exclude an aspirated object

medicines.generic_name: No routine medicine for mechanical choking
medicines.role: Foreign-body obstruction is treated with age-appropriate first aid and airway management, not tablets or home remedies.
medicines.safety: Do not give oral medicines, food or liquids during active choking.

medicines.role: May be used by clinicians for hypoxaemia or concurrent bronchospasm after airway assessment; does not remove an obstruction.
medicines.safety: Never substitute for clearing a severe obstruction or emergency airway management.

diagnostic_process: Age-appropriate first aid and emergency response
Evaluate persistent symptoms or suspected aspiration; specialist assessment may be needed

sources.name: American Heart Association (AHA)
sources.title: Part 7: Adult Basic Life Support (2025 AHA Guidelines)

source_note: First-aid recommendations may differ slightly by jurisdiction and guideline edition; use the locally adopted resuscitation standard.
